utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. A few procedural matters. I do understand that there is a stipulation between the Prosecution and the Gotovina Defence with the following content. Milan Ramljak was Vice Prime Minister of Croatia between the 3rd of August, 1991, and the 12th of August, 1992. He was Croatia's ambassador to Austria between 21st December, 1993, and the 14th of May, 1998. He then held the position of Croatia's Minister Of Justice from 14th of May, 1998, to the 13th of April, 1999, and he was not a member of the Croatian government in 1995. I hear of no objection. Therefore, it is now put on the record that at least the Gotovina Defence and the Prosecution stipulated these facts. If any of the other parties would take distance of it, I would like to hear. Otherwise the Chamber will assume that these facts are not contested by the other Defence teams. Mr. Mikulicic, you would like to make submissions in relation to client/counsel privileged -- privilege in relation The Blue Book. You have an opportunity to do so. And could you indicate how much time would you need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, not more than ten minutes, let's say, or maybe less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will continue in Croatian, if the Court pleases. [Interpretation] Your Honours, the issue was raised of The Blue Book and the material which the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia handed over to the Defence team for General Markac. I will only have a few points to raise to inform the Trial Chamber of the events preceding. On the 16th of July, 2007, the Defence for General Markac got in touch through the Office for Cooperation with the ICTY, the Office For Cooperation of the Republic of Croatia, with the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, with a request to be supplied certain materials from the archives, and the request to make available to the Defence team all the documents and information related to Operation Storm 1995. Based on our request, the Office For Cooperation with the ICTY sent to the Defence for General Markac the material sought and the analysis of Operation Storm 1995 which was in fact The Blue Book that was discussed, and it sent all the material on the 2nd of August, 2007. The material was delivered in hard copy and on CDs. The Defence for General Markac considers the material to fall under Rule 67 of the Rules, in view of the fact that The Blue Book is material that the Defence for General Markac did not -- did not consider, and did not want to, and will not use in its own case. According to the position of the team for General Markac, the material, i.e., The Blue Book, also falls under the remit of Rule 70, since it had been prepared at the request of the Defence in the process of collecting material to be used before the Tribunal for Defence purposes. However, with the intention of being of assistance to the Chamber and the parties to the proceedings, the Defence team will distribute to everyone the electronic copy of The Blue Book, as we received it from the Office For Cooperation with the ICTY which had received it from the MOD, in an attempt to assist the Trial Chamber in the current proceedings. I repeat, this material is -- will not be used by the Defence. It had never been the intention of the team to use it. It was working material which the team for General Markac has decided to make available to all the parties to the proceedings that may wish to have a look at it. We have prepared the original version of the letter we received from the Office for Cooperation with the ICTY, dated the 2nd of August, whereby the material was delivered to the Defence. Of course, the letter has not been translated since it is working material of the Defence. We have it on the screen. We will also show the cover page of The Blue Book, wherein it is stated that the analysis of Operation Storm was compiled on the request of the Defence team for Colonel General Markac, based on the decision of the minister of defence, which we were able to look at yesterday, and which lists all the individuals who, on behalf of the MOD, worked on the compilation of The Blue Book. I would kindly ask the Registry now to show us the letter dated the 2nd of August, 2007, via Sanction, and then I will -- I kindly ask that the cover page be placed on the ELMO, which explains the -- how the book came about and the persons involved in the making of it. This, Your Honours, is the letter from the Office for Cooperation with international courts within the Ministry of Justice addressed to the Defence team for General Markac, wherein it is stated that we are being sent the analysis of Operation Storm which is The Blue Book, and wherein they inform us that they are also sending us supporting documentation with maps contained within four binders, as well as the CD containing the documents, i.e., The Blue Book, and it is in fact the CD that we will be distributing to the parties. Your Honour, should you so wish, we may go through the entire document with the assistance of the interpreters, but I don't think that it is necessary. We merely wanted to show you the procedure whereby we came in -- into the possession of The Blue Book that was discussed here yesterday. If you have any questions on this score, I will gladly answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be very practical. The concern expressed by Mr. Kay is whether, by providing The Blue Book there would be any violation of client/counsel privilege, whether that would be a rule which makes an exception to disclosure obligations, whether it would be Rule 70, whether it is work product or not. It's a rather complex situation where, well, there is a request, then a committee is formed, and other people are attending. So to what extent this exactly falls within the scope of internal work product, and to what extent it also touches upon Rule 97, which says that if there's any protected or confidential communication between counsel and client, but if this has been disclosed to third parties, that those third parties can give evidence on that. We can leave all that for the time being alone, I think, because what you're offering is, We'll provide you with The Blue Book. Which means that, certainly, whatever the confidentiality may be, that, at least, under Rule 97, your client has consented to such disclosure. At least I take it that your position is based on consent of your client. Which, for the time being, I think eliminates all problematic, possible problematic aspects of such disclosure. And, therefore, unless other parties would disagree with this observation, I think that we appreciate that you offered assistance to providing The Blue Book, either the Chamber or the parties, at least the parties, but perhaps it -- and I leave that to some extent to the parties as well. The Chamber has not made up its mind as to whether we would like to call that documentary evidence as Chamber evidence. Of course, if the parties would present it as evidence, then, of course, there would be no need for the Chamber to even consider such an initiative. So, therefore, for the time being, we'll wait what the parties will do. It will be made available. It is not only the Markac Defence but now all parties that have access to this material. We will see what happens, and we will consider the position of the Chamber in view of the -- of the course of events that will follow, in relation to this Blue Book. Any need to make further submissions on the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. One route occurs to me, is it may be appropriate, and I would be seeking this having now been acquainted with the material overnight and wanting to use it on behalf of my client, a stipulation route as to the content of the material as a way of dealing with evidentiary problems, i.e., the reference to General Cermak in the book, making a stipulation between the parties as to what that single reference in whole book is, and that occurs to me as being a -- a middle route that might serve justice as well as protect privilege on the basis that there has been disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As I said before, the Chamber will see how the parties will deal with the now available material. And I do understand that you -- you have not yet talked to the other parties in relation to a possible stipulation, but you will try to achieve such a stipulation at shortest notice, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I mentioned to Mr. Waespi information that had been given to me. I was acquainted with it overnight. I'm grateful for Mr. Mikulicic's assistance and statement this morning. It occurs to me that if I start re-examining on the content of it, I may be causing a problem within the proceedings that we could otherwise avoid, but it -- if I suggest, as I have to the Court and to other parties that that may be a -- a route to solve a problem, I put it out there so that everyone knows that I'm interested in dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, of course, the Chamber, not aware of the content of the material, let alone any -- any mentioning of Mr. Cermak in that material, of course, would encourage the parties to deal with it as quickly as possible, because Mr. Feldi is now here, but he will not remain here forever. At least that's what the Chamber expects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honours encouragement. That is what I was seeking because obviously the witness is here for a limited amount of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would you think that the next break would be the appropriate moment, or would you say give us 15 minutes now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, I think it's something that -- materials that could be looked at and something in the break worked out between the parties and -- I think that's the best route.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, I see some eyebrows being raised to my left; that is, the Prosecution. Let's see what can be achieved; and if nothing can be achieved, we'll hear that. I do understand that if the material has been produced overnight, I've got no idea whether it's a small blue book or a big blue book, I have no idea. I leave it, at this moment, to the parties to see whether the suggestion made by Mr. Kay is a viable route or not. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, good morning. The Prosecution is similarly in the dark. We haven't seen it, so we don't know anything about it, whether it has been translated, et cetera. Just to alert the Court to that issue from the get-go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Kay apparently found his way overnight to have not only access to it but even such an access that he was able to -- apparently able to understand what was in The Blue Book. I leave it at this moment to the parties. There is no role for the Chamber at this moment, apart from encouraging to seek solutions for whatever problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I could foresee that lack of translation could be a problem. As I said, this document was not mentioned to be introduced as an evidence as it regards to Markac Defence. Therefore, it is on Croatian language. And the material is -- well, there is a -- quite an amount of the material, so I don't think that the translation could be completed within a short period. But, nevertheless, here is the CD with the material, and I would like to share with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So if I may have the assistance of Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you -- this is visible disclosure for the Chamber. The Chamber is never a witness to disclosure, but now we see how it works. Mr. Carrier, I'm leaving behind me -- I see even how disclosure is distributed within the Prosecution's team physically. It's a new experience for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What I meant is one CD per each Defence and one CD for the Prosecution side and one CD for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now the Chamber is a witness as well as where it goes wrong with disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as we, I believe, completed this discussion, just for Your Honour I would like to show via ELMO the cover page, the first page of the book which contains the members who participate in obtaining this document, so that that could be also transparent and visible to the OTP and other parties and to the Chamber of course as well. So some of the names were mentioned yesterday, if Your Honour remembers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see Lovric, Feldi, Pokaz, Bartolac, Skuliber, Sambolec apparently as members of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. And then the other group below has been composed by Mr. Mihevc, Sertic, and Stojanovic. And they were only included into the working group but not the members of the working group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They participated in the work of the group without being members. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's all, Your Honour, I have to say. If you have any questions, I will be glad do answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then move on. Mr. Carrier, the Chamber yesterday seriously considered whether it had to cut down the time for further cross-examination. The credibility issues yesterday took far more time than was really needed to establish or to seek to establish what you wanted to establish. After thorough reflection, the Chamber decided not to do that, but may this be a flag for the future. Get to the core of what is at stake more quickly. Therefore, you said you would need four sessions. Well, we have spent now quite a bit of time on this procedural issue. Therefore, in all fairness, the Chamber grants you but will strictly keep you to that time-limit - one hour and a half - for further cross-examination. Madam Usher, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be very practical, perhaps the parties could focus. Apparently Mr. Kay takes it that the name of Mr. Cermak is mentioned only once, and then with reservation of other rights to say, well, on that portion we would agree on what it says apart from that it could be taken out of context, et cetera, but at least that we focus as much as possible on what could be achieved when the witness is still there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Feldi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. And Mr. Carrier will now continue his cross-examination. May I also ask you again to focus your answers on what is asked. Further details if any parties are interested in it, they will certainly ask for it. But let's start with a focussed answer to the question. Please proceed, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, am I correct in saying that you had free range to a database that contained basically a -- most of the documents, at least a huge number of documents related to this case and that included witness testimony and witness statements?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, in fact, in your report itself you reference on one page the evidence of General Lausic. You reference both his statement and his testimony. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review all of General Lausic's testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, I did follow directly his testimony before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Feldi, you're aware, then, that the Prosecution's position in this case is that the military police units were subordinated to HV commanders during Operation Storm and throughout the remainder of 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that -- that's a question that can be put. Are we relying on General Lausic's testimony or the Prosecution case? I think it needs some clarity here, because there are two distinctive issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understood that Mr. Carrier was inquiring whether, perhaps on the basis of having listened to questions and answers put to Mr. Lausic whether the witness was aware of what the Prosecution's case, in this respect, was. That is, that the military police units were subordinated to HV commanders during Operation Storm throughout the remainder of 1995. Is that correct, Mr. Carrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are you aware that that's the Prosecution's case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not aware that that was the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then now you are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asked now whether I was aware of that. I'm -- I can only say that I'm sorry that that doesn't seem to be the right case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, may I also invite the parties not to intervene unnecessarily, also in view of the time-limits that are imposed on Mr. Carrier. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Feldi, having watched and followed the testimony of General Lausic, a Prosecution witness, you're saying you didn't understand that that was the Prosecution's position then; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, I did not understand it to be that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, in that vein, then, Mr. Feldi, you have referenced a number of documents in your report to support your position which is that the military police were not in fact subordinated to HV commanders as the Prosecution asserts. And a number of those documents -- and I will go through some of them. One is Exhibit P880 [Realtime transcript read in error "P808"] which are the rules governing the structure an operation of the military police. Those are the 1994 rules. You also reference D267, which is a 2 August 1995 order from General Lausic. That's in relation to preparing military police units to perform military police tasks in the areas of responsibility of the Croatian Army during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, I think you said P880. If I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, P -- sorry. The transcript is wrong. It's P880.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Exhibit P881, which is a 5 August 1995 order, again issued by General Lausic in respect of establishing military police units in the newly liberated areas of Croatia, as well as D47, which is a 14 August 1995 order, again issued by General Lausic. This one is in respect of implementation of military police tasks in the zones of responsibility of the military police units. Now, is it also your position that you're unaware that the Prosecution has taken a contrary view to your interpretation of those documents in respect of military police subordination, and the Prosecution's position is that these documents actually support the premise that military police units were subordinated to HV commanders during Operation Storm and throughout 1995? Were you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of the Prosecution's case and conclusions. I only followed the witness testimonies and read the documents that you have just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: But having followed General Lausic's testimony, you are aware that - and if I can just be direct - the Prosecution's position is the same as General Lausic's regarding those documents, that in fact HV units were subordinated -- or, sorry, MP units were subordinated to HV units during that time. So is that clear to you now?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not. I don't know what made you infer that. That is why it is unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Feldi, I'm not asking you to evaluate the inference at the moment. I'm just asking you if now you're aware of the fact that the Prosecution's position is that General Lausic's -- with respect to those documents, that you cite over and over in your report, that General Lausic dealt with during his testimony. Are you aware of that, that -- now you're fully aware that that's the Prosecution's position regarding those documents?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Feldi, your report does not explicitly refer to additional pieces of evidence that the Prosecution also relies on to support its position in this respect regarding command and control over MP units. And in that vain I want to just direct your attention to a few examples from the evidence of General Lausic which you said you looked at, and then I'll have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Completely cognizant of the Chamber's admonition about rising and interrupting, but the continuous use of the phrase, The Prosecution's position that the command and control was with the HV commanders, I don't believe that is has been the Prosecution's case to this point, and it is a term of art to say command and control was with HV units. There is a distinction between command and command and control, and to this point, unless the Prosecutor will point me specifically to where command and control was given to HV commanders in the field, I'm going to object to posing the question without any foundation in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I might be able to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, when I referred to command and control over MP units in the field, what I'm specifically referring to, just -- is that the MP units were subordinated to HV commanders for the performance of their military police tasks in the -- in the operational zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think we've been through this issue before, and those are not the same synonymous terminology. And so I would ask that with an expert witness that the terminology be accurate in terms of what the evidence is on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be -- what the evidence is in the record, the witness told us that he has followed that evidence. If Mr. Carrier would put portions of that evidence to the witness, then I think we avoid any confusion in this respect, and that's what I thought Mr. Carrier would do. Therefore, Mr. Carrier, let's stay away from whatever terms that are in dispute, and let's see what the comment of the witness is, as you suggest you do, to certain portions of the evidence of Mr. Lausic, material which has been used and considered by him when preparing the report. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, the first one is D567. This is an analysis of the use of MPs during Operation Storm. It's dated 16 September 1995, and it was sent to, among others, the Chief of the Main Staff, Cervenko; Defence Minister Susak and General Gotovina. It was sent by General Lausic. In that report, he reported that daily operational command by commanders of the HV Military District was one of the things that made it possible to carry out all police tasks within the competence of the military police. Mr. Lausic, during his testimony, stated that Article 9 envisaged the right to implement daily operational tasks in everyday activities to the various commanders of the armed forces in Croatia. General Lausic also stated during his testimony HV unit commanders or garrison commanders within those area of responsibility of specific MP unit is, Command MP to executed all military policing tasks in keeping the authority and -- in keeping with the authority and work of the military police. They are also tasked with daily monitoring of the work of the MP and to notify the MP administration with the proposal of measures to be undertaken by the administration so as to ensure efficient functioning of the MP unit. General Lausic also testified that the 72nd Battalion MP Company based in Knin was subordinated to the highest military commander in his area of responsibility --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's a misquote, as we know, from the -- the test is by function. I'm a bit concerned about it being read out this way. I don't want do be obstructive, Your Honour, but I would appreciate references. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was about to find it where exactly. If you give the page reference, then we are able to follow that. And then, of course, in order to use your time as efficiently as possible, it would be wise to not summarize or quote in any way which would cause other parties to object.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, I guess in that respect, Your Honour, I'm not sure, if Mr. Kay doesn't know where it is from. I don't know how he says it is a misquote. But I'll identify it. It is P2159, paragraphs 194 to 195.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And just to finish that off, he said that: "... which was the town of Knin and surrounding area and the highest ranking Croatian Army commander in Knin at that time was General Cermak." That same document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We should rely on the evidence as well because he was cross-examined and gave testimony. And I'm concerned with -- with a one-eyed look at evidence this way and claiming it represents his testimony. Your Honour, perhaps it can be done a different way, by asking the witness questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I think there is no duty for Mr. Carrier to put all the related evidence to a certain issue to this witness. At the same time, Mr. Carrier, it's not very efficient and effective if you ignore that portion of the testimony that stems from cross-examination. Therefore, I would not -- I wouldn't disallow you to put to the witness what Mr. Lausic said, if it is not a -- if it does not reflect the core of his testimony, the whole of his testimony on this matter, then please refrain from saying, This is the testimony of, but you could say, Mr. Lausic said this or that, and then later Mr. Kay can put to the witness what else has been said by Mr. Lausic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, and if I can just respond, Your Honour. Mr. Kay's objection is basically, if I'm understanding it correctly, is that what he'd like to put to him during re-direct, and that is clearly open to him, the point being, I've given the limited time and describing it as testimony simply is based on the fact that he said it during his testimony or he put it in his statement. And so to object the first time saying that it should be quoting, and then to suggest in the next objection which follows on the heels of that one saying that I should be summarizing it to give an accurate reflection of everything that Mr. Kay would like in the parts that I'm reading, it, frankly, with respect, doesn't make any sense. So I'm just trying to put things to him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, in my ruling on what you are allowed to do or not to do is not already what you now say reflected in that ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes. [Overlapping speakers] ... I'm just responding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore -- yes, well, if the ruling is there, there is no need to respond at that moment. If I consider that I could give a ruling which is, to some extent, in your favour, just in order to save time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, another thing that General Lausic indicated was that the Knin MP company was under General Cermak's command for its day-to-day activities and that if a crime was committed within his area of responsibility, it would be his responsibility to direct the military police. And General Lausic also testified that MP subordination granted to HV commanders under Article 9 of the 1994 rules was, in effect, the same system of command and control over military police as described in the December 1992 Military Council. And moving away from General Lausic briefly, General Cermak, himself, in his 2004 interview stated that General Gotovina had the entire military police under him. Now, first, Mr. Feldi, very simply, can you just please tell the Court whether or not you specifically considered any of these specific examples, pieces of information that I have read to you in relation to the issue of MP subordination when you conducted your analysis in your report?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, I did, and in detail too. When searching for documents, I tried to find at least a single document that would corroborate what you are saying; I did not, however. But, on the other hand, I found at least five other documents which show the contrary, which is that the MP company in Knin was never subordinated to the Knin garrison commander by virtue of any orders. It was only Lausic who said so. I didn't find any documents to corroborate that. The following example testifies to that. In Article 9 under Rules --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because my question was -- my question was very simple. It was whether or not you specifically considered any of those specific examples. And you said that you had and that you did that in detail. Now, if that's the case, where in your report do you reference that or make that transparent that you considered these things in detail; specifically those pieces of evidence, if you can find any of them. And while you're looking, I'm going suggest to you, Mr. Feldi, you're not going to find them in your report because they are not in your report specifically referenced.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, I don't know whether you studied my report in detail. I do know, however, that I referred to the report you mentioned of the 16th of September, in which General Lausic sends a report on the functioning of the military police during Operation Storm. Therein, he confirms that the commander, General Stipetic, commanded the MP unit pursuant to the order of the chief of MP administration. Nowhere in the report does he say that the MP company in Knin was commanded by General Cermak. Such a position is simply not present in the report, and this is what I state in my report. There is no order issued by General Lausic referenced in my report --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because what I'm asking you is specifically the part of that report you're now going through and referencing General Stipetic. I'm asking you whether and where exactly precisely in your report you consider in detail the part where General Lausic reports to Cervenko, Susak, and Gotovina about the command part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I object to the -- to the formulation of the question. I don't think he reported to General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, whether it's reporting or whether it's communicating on these matters is not the key issue here. So could you please ask -- answer the question without focussing on whether it was a real report or a report in, I would say, in technical terms. But Mr. Carrier would like to hear from you where exactly in your report you'll consider in detail the Lausic communication with Cervenko, Susak, and Gotovina about command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in chapter 3, the relationship between Colonel General Cermak with the military police in the area of the Knin garrison, under items 3.2.1, 3.2.2, 3.2.3, 3.2.4, 3.2.5, 3.2.6, and 3.2.7. These are documents referenced in footnotes 179 through to and including 188.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could ask a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your previous question where we would find in the report a certain matter has been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: What I'd like to know, then, Mr. Feldi, specifically where is it that you're, in detail, discussing that specific portion of General Lausic's analysis? Because I can't see it, at least, in the sections that you're talking about, where you specifically reference that and talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, apparently the question is where you gave your expert opinion on certain matters on the basis of the material footnoted, whether and where to find in the report that you specifically and in detail addressed the testimony of Mr. Lausic in this respect. That's apparently what you would like to know, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in item 1.5.12, and 1.5.13, documents D02159 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure about the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the numbers, because they might have been misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P02159 and P02159 [as interpreted], in footnote 72. And the transcript of testimony which I have under the number that we used of the 27th January 2009. In that section, I refer to items 18 and 19 of the statement and witness testimony in connection with the documents we discussed yesterday. His supervision of the units in the operational areas of the 91st, and the preparations and development of the first set of rules governing the work of the military police. In chapter 3 that I referred to earlier, I do not specifically reference Lausic's statements and testimony. Rather, I'm -- I refer to the documents that he produced; the orders and reports that he sent. These documents do not corroborate the position that the MP units, in accordance with Article 9 of the rules governing the work of the military police, were subordinated to the HV commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could interject because given my limited time and given that that isn't an answer to my specific question, I'll leave it there and I'll move on, but what he is talking is obviously not an answer to the question. So if I could just move on to the next point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's not a complete answer to the question. I leave it to you. What I noticed is that, for example, the -- that sometimes footnoted material is referred to by its 65 ter number, which specifically, if attention is drawn to certain paragraphs in which we find such footnotes, that the Chamber has no access to 65 ter material. So to the parties - and I'm also addressing you, Mr. Kay, in this respect - should find a solution for that, that the Chamber is not paralysed by having no access to the sources apparently used by the expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and Your Honour did ask for focus cases, and General Feldi could have written a 500 page report, no doubt, quoting everything and -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Le me just -- I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- saying that. But if reference is made to a specific paragraph which contains reference to such source material, there, of course, in order to evaluate the testimony in relation to that specific paragraph and the specific sources used in that paragraph, there, I think, we would have to find a solution. Please proceed, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, I'm going turn your attention now to paragraph 1.5.22 of your report, which is on page 30 in English and page 27 in the B/C/S. In this part of your report, you indicate that the minister of defence issued special orders that established the authorities of the military police administration, and you also maintain that -- that in these orders the obligation that all military police units be subordinate only to the military police administration was part of it. And in that respect, you -- you reference two specific orders, the first being Exhibit D35, which is Defence Minister Susak's order dated 6 July 1994, and you cite that in respect of, among other things, as I said, removing -- or, sorry, what the order is about in the title and when he talks about it -- in -- Minister Susak is that the goal is to remove ambiguity in a system of command and control over units of the military police. And the other order from Minister Susak you reference is P2175, which is a Minister Susak order dated 7 August 1995, which is after the launch of Operation Storm. And that one is in respect of, among other things, physical security of warehousing facilities in the liberated territories. Now, Mr. Feldi, when you conducted your analysis, did you or did you not specifically -- specifically consider General Lausic's explanation that he provided regarding these two orders issued by Minister Susak?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, the orders are by the Defence Minister on securing the warehouses of 7 August 1995 only makes incumbent upon the MP to secure all the storage facilities. In the order of --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, I'm going to cut you off because I have limited time. My question is, when you conducted your analysis, did you or did you not specifically consider General Lausic's explanation for these two orders issued by Minister Susak?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I had General Lausic's order. I had the document under footnote 90, which is document D75. General Lausic issued his order as soon as he received the minister's order. To me, this is a piece of evidence showing how the system worked. In the testimony or statement by Mr. Lausic, I did not find anywhere his explanation as to why he took the course he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, first, you referred to footnote 90, and there it appears on the transcript that you would have said document D75. But in footnote 90, a reference is made to D795. And I would like to add to that that your answer seems to be a bit confusing because the question simply was whether you considered the explanation given by Mr. Lausic. Your answer was: No, I didn't, because I could look at the document itself. And then you start explaining that you did not find anything in his explanation, why he took the course he did. Well, there's a contradiction between your first answer that you didn't consider it, and then you explain what you found when you considered his explanation. So that's a bit confusing for me. Mr. Carrier, being aware of this confusion, I don't know whether you want to further clarify it. Apparently the witness, in the second part of his answer, said that he did consider it, but he did not find a satisfactory explanation of the final conclusions drawn by Mr. Lausic. If you want to further explore it, fine; but, if not, fine as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I don't think there is any purpose in going further with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, despite your suggestion to the contrary in your report, can you specifically point to what it is in the 1994 rules governing the military police that explicitly states that Article 9, in and of itself, does not produce direct results, or that Article 9 requires some kind of implementing order?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, in the last item of the rules governing the work of the MP, it is stated that the application and the interpretation of the rules would be determined by the MP administration. In my view, the MP administration was also duty-bound to regulate the application of Article 9 of the rules. In other words, at what time and under what circumstances the HV commanders would be given powers to carry out certain tasks. This is something that I did not find anywhere in the MP administration that they invoked Article 9 in order to confer the power upon the HV commanders to have command over MP units, and this is something that I highlighted in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So that specific item that you're referring to, because in your opinion, the military police administration had -- had done nothing, that the regulations themselves didn't just take effect, given that they were -- when they were signed, it also says that they take effect as of the date of signing them?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So you're just assuming that there should be some kind of regulation that says that there needs to be implementing orders or that there needs to be some kind of grant from the military police administration in order for HV commanders to have subordination of MP units in the field? You're assuming that; that that should have happened?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, this is not an assumption on my part. We're discussing a document, which is the rules of the military police and not the rules governing the Croatian Army. The rules of the MP indicate that the chief of the MP administration is not entitled to have command over the HV. Therefore, what is stated in the rules makes it incumbent upon the MP administration to regulate when the MP units would be under the command of the HV commanders. Nothing in the rules mentions the general regulations concerning the Croatian Army, the brigade commanders, operational areas, et cetera. This is a piece of regulations. If Article 9 say says MP units can be subordinated to Article 9 in performing regular military police duties, military police units shall be subordinated to the commanders of the Military Districts, commanders of the navy, of the air force; that is to say, to the most senior commander of the Croatian Army, in the area where the military police unit is active. That's Article 9. Therefore, as can you see, according to Article 9 in the performance of regular military police duties, military police units shall be subordinated to the commanders of the Croatian Army. However, in Article 10, I didn't find anywhere the definition of the military police duties. Article 10 states or references areas of activity and military police duties. There is no mention of any extraordinary, exceptional daily or other types of tasks of the military police. In other words, what is relevant is the area where the MP unit is present. And as for the tasks that the military police units carry -- carry out, this isn't something that was so defined in Article 9. Now, in the order that General Lausic sends to the various MP units, no mention is made of these regular military police duties that -- or where HV commanders would come in. That's why I referenced the order concerning the securing of storage facilities, because in them, in that order, no duties or obligations were mentioned of the HV units. In fact, HV units didn't have anything to do with these securing or other tasks because they fell within the purview of the military police. That was my understanding and interpretation of the situation, if I have made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see whether I understood the main issue in dispute. It seems that Mr. Feldi says Article 9 needs further implementation; it's not self-executing. We find no further regulations on it. Therefore, it could not, in itself, directly apply. Whereas, as the absence of further implementing regulations is understood by others as demonstrating that, in fact, Article 9 was self-executing. That seems to be the issue, if -- if that's clear, then we could go on for ages to interpret the absence of further implementing regulatory instruments, and then go back again and again to that the absence demonstrates, on the one hand, that it wasn't effective, it was not ever implemented; and the other view, that it's this very absence that demonstrates that it was directly applicable. That seems to be the issue. The Chamber is fully aware of the issue. It's not for the first time that we deal with Article 9, Article 10, what it explains, what it doesn't explain. The issue is clear. If Mr. Feldi would like to add anything to this analysis or to bring to our attention a striking point which would underline the correctness of his interpretation, he has an opportunity to do so in the next minute; and, otherwise, I think we should move on. Mr. Feldi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I referenced this in several sections of my report, and I provided, I believe, detailed explanations which do not warrant any additional submissions on that. Thank you. I think I was precise enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Carrier, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, you returned to the issue of warehousing. And what you said in that respect was that -- if I understand you correctly, that because there were being -- orders being issued with respect to that -- and is it your position that that's a regular military police task, guarding those warehouses?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, I didn't say that it was one of their regular duties. They were ordered to do that, under the decision or the order of the Ministry of Defence. And whatever the duty, the military police have to carry out orders. In Article 10, among their duties, they have the securing of lives; therefore, of persons, and properties, vital properties, in this instance, they were MOD warehouses placed at the disposal of the army, and this is why the minister issued the decision whereby the military police was supposed to secure all the warehouses in the liberated areas. When the order was issued, the chief of the MP administration proceeded to issue his own order on the same day or on the following day, addressed to the commanders in the field to take upon themselves the security detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... simple question: Did you, or do you consider this task to be performed, as ordered, to be within the regular military police tasks? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said at the outset that I didn't know what the regular tasks were, because I didn't find the definition of it in any of the regulations. What is prescribed is the area of activity and tasks, which could be regular and exceptional or extraordinary. And it is true that this is the provision of Article 10 of the rules governing the work of the MP. And it was on this basis that the minister issued his decision, and the chief of the MP administration, his order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: We'll move on from there, Mr. Feldi. Yesterday you mentioned at transcript page T21926, lines 18 to 22, that you had submitted a draft report to Mr. Kay and that he had made comments on it, which you took into consideration for your final draft. My question is: As a result of those comments from Mr. Kay, did you add, delete, or modify anything in the draft report before you submitted a final report?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, the first version of my manuscript - it wasn't a final version - numbered some 180 -- 180 pages and had many documents apprehended. When Mr. Kay received the copy, he told me that he accepted the contents as such, but he wanted the report to be reduced to some 50 to 60 pages without specifying what it is that I should add or omit. When I produced the version of the report which you have before you now, he accepted the report with some minor stylistic or linguistic changes and told me to hand over the final version, which I did in July. It was on the basis of his request dating from February this year that I produced the report in the course of four to five months and submitted it to him for review, for his consideration. And the material, with all the supporting documents and material, is still in my possession as well as, of course, the copies that were handed over to Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, there was no question about whether any earlier versions were still in your possession. I do understand, and that would have been a short answer, that you reduced the size of the report, because Mr. Kay considered it too long for the purposes, that he did not give you any instructions or requests as far as the substance, the content of it was concerned, apart from reducing the size, and that for the next version, there was only a request to improve some stylistic elements. Is that ... if that is your answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. Thank you. I apologise for belabouring the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's try to keep ourselves focussed on what is asked. And it was not asked who had kept copies. If Mr. Carrier wants to know, he will ask you. Please proceed, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, if you could turn to page -- paragraph 1.3.14 of your report, which is on page 18 in English and 16 in B/C/S, you state there that it is utterly inadequate and legally unfounded to refer to the concept of command and control as articulated in the 1990 JNA ground forces regulations or the US Army FM 101-5 to draw any conclusions about the command and control over the HV since these principles are, you say, in contradiction with the command laws and regulations implemented in the HV. Mr. Feldi, can you specifically direct to us what parts of these two documents you reference, the 1990 JNA regulations and the US Army manual that are in contradiction to the extent that they render any conclusions utterly inadequate and legally unfounded vis-a-vis command and control of the HV?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, quite specifically, the rules of service of the Croatian Army were written for the purposes of the Croatian Army. In the JNA, there was the rules of service of the JNA. The rules of service of the JNA provided for its rules and regulations to be applied in times of war, when it comes to documents and regulations that had -- that were applicable to combat activities. Under such circumstances, tasks would be regulated in accordance with these rules applicable in war. When we were drafting our rules of service, we left those parts out because they were contrary to the principles underlying the Croatian Army. This is the specific example of the instant issue. The second specific example is the comparisons drawn between garrison commanders and JNA commanders of town defence structures. In the HV, garrisons are prescribed and no provisions were included regulating the defence of garrisons or the defence of towns. In the JNA rules of service, mention is made of garrison commands which even have the right to engage in mobilizations as well as those in charge of the defence of towns. Similar principles are applied in the Russian army. This was particularly mentioned by Mr. Theunens. I hope this is the answer to your question, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: That's -- time for the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's time for the break. We resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, please proceed. From my body language you will see what is on my mind as well. Looking in a certain direction. No, not to Mr. Kay. I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Oh. Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The clock is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I wear a watch, so I was looking at that, but I will move as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, the Prosecution asserts that the reality of the situation on the ground is -- in fact, reflects that the applicability of Article 9 was as -- as testified to by General Lausic, and the Prosecution' position is that the MP were subordinated to General Cermak as well as General Gotovina. Now, in your report, if I have understood it correctly, your position is that General Cermak's orders to both the civilian police and the military police were simply to provide information and that they were not actually meant to engage them in carrying out any tasks. Is that right? That's your position in your report?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Feldi, the Prosecution asserts that in fact a number of the document, some of them that you refer to, reflect General Cermak's authority to issue orders to both the military police and the civilian police. And I just want to review a few of those orders as well as some of the responses in relation to orders that were issued by the Knin garrison command or -- or that indicate that General Cermak was issuing orders to these people. Number one -- and for reference is for my friends, it's P513. I don't intend to bring them up, but I'll just summarize them. They are one-page documents. Sorry, this one, actually, is an order by General Cermak dated 8 August 1995 regards freedom of movement for UNCRO elements. It's addressed to the MUP, Knin police station as well as to the military police. It's called an order. It's signed by General Cermak. And it's to take effect immediately. Another document that the Prosecution relies on this in respect is the log-book of the 72nd Military Police Battalion. That log-book has an entry dated 11 August 1995, at 11.50 a.m., which indicates that the 72nd Military Police Battalion duty officer informed regarding a command of General Cermak that members of UNCRO have complete freedom of movement. And these are just examples, Mr. Feldi. But P509, this is an order by General Cermak dated 15 August 1995 regarding unhindered access for civilians at all military and civilian police check-points. That order was addressed to the Knin police station as well as to the Knin military police. It's called an order, and it also says that it is to take effect immediately. And P510, this is a follow-up by the chief of the Kotar-Knin police administration, and ... page 2 of that document in English says -- and I'm just going to pause for a moment. "We received an order from the Knin Military District, Croatian army command, commanding us to ensure that from 15 August 1995 all civilians pass freely through all military and police check-points on the roads into Knin, ensure that the civilian population can enter the town of Knin without permits. Checks shall continue in accordance with previously stated rules." And, finally, Mr. Feldi, P1147; this is an 8 September 1995 letter from General Cermak apologising to a member of the European Mission regarding impermissible behaviour of a person in a Croatian Army uniform. And in that letter, General Cermak indicates that he has issued an order to the military police to investigate. Now my question to you, Mr. Feldi, having looked at some of these pieces of information, when you drew your conclusions with respect to how the orders of General Cermak should be regarded in relation to military police and the civilian police, how do you -- how do you account for the fact that the documents issued are called orders. They're received, according to some of the information I just gave you, received by members of the military police and civilian police who, it seems to indicate, execute those orders, how is it that you can maintain your position that they're only for information purposes, in light of that information?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, it was my conclusion that this was information or notifications sent by the Knin garrison commander to the military police, the civilian police, and others. First of all, he had no operational command authority, pursuant to the organisational order, item 3. He is not authorised to command the military police. As for the orders you are referring to as documents, are not operational orders. Having analysed these orders, I concluded that they do not meet the basic criteria of operational command. An order, or, rather, the orders he issued, were not written by a soldier. One can deduce that. It wasn't put together by a military officer with an operational background and training. For example, in those orders there is no obligation mentioned of the subordinates having to inform on the implementation. Then others are addressed in unusual ways. For example, instead of addressing a document to the 72nd MP Battalion or the Independent Joint Company, as it was referred to by various MP officers in their report, when writing to them he simply addresses that to the military police. He didn't address his orders to the chief of the police station in Knin but to the civilian police in general. Having analysed the orders, I realized that those orders were written ad hoc, if I may say so, in order to keep them informed, and he never received any feedback information on the implementation. There is not a single report of anyone responding to General Cermak's orders to the effect that they had been implemented and measures put in place to prevent such occurrences in the future. I did not come across a single instance of such an order. That is why I concluded that these were merely notifications without placing a burden on anyone to implement them. Concerning the orders issued by the Knin garrison commander in the various reports of the MP units to their superior commands, there is not a single mention of that. For example, the commander of the 72nd MP Battalion sending reports to Zagreb never mentions that he had ever received an order of the Knin garrison commander and followed it through. We have a situation the other way around in which the garrison commander is complaining that the MP units which received the same orders as the civilian police did not care to implement them. I don't know whether this answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I could just ask you one clarifying question. If it is for information purposes, what's the point in -- in putting in the order that's directed to military police and civilian police that it takes effect immediately? Is it your position that the information is to take effect immediately or ...

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The obligations of the garrison commanders, it is stated that certain issues are to be regulated by providing information, drafting instructions, and issuing orders. When it comes to the relationship between the garrison commander and the military police units in the area of the garrison, in item 4 of the instruction on the work in garrisons, the garrison commander is duty-bound to put in place cooperation and coordination with MP units in their policing tasks. That is to say, he had no right to order an MP unit. For that reason, he simply sent informational reports to them or instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I am going cut you off because it was just about what the purpose was of making it take effect immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Carrier. Mr. Kay, is there any need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- further examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: General Feldi, you were asked questions about The Blue Book, and you were shown a document that we won't produce on the screen that was Exhibit P2632, marked for identification, and under seal. You remember looking at that document, being taken through it by Mr. Carrier yesterday?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it concerned the production of an analysis on Operation Oluja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In that document you looked at, was there any allegation that you had done anything unlawful; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, as far as I understand, in the document there isn't even my name or -- first or last name. In the document, it is stated that, for the analysis of Operation Storm, it would be General Lovric and General Repinc who would be engaged in working on that. I'm not present. I do not figure. I don't know where the misunderstanding came from. I kindly asked the Tribunal that I receive the decision of the Ministry of Defence from August 2007, in which my name is mentioned as a team member of the committee tasked with making that analysis. There are those people who Mr. Carrier mentioned yesterday as having participated. When we were working on the document, we did not have a indictment and we did not making our analysis based on. That we were completely ignorant of any indictments. I hope this answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was just a simple question requiring yes or no. Was there any allegation in the documents you looked at yesterday that you had done anything unlawful?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was none.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was there any allegation in any of the documents that you looked at yesterday that you had done anything dishonest; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the document itself referred to as The Blue Book, have you read that document in full?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour -- or Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to tell the Court the number of times that Mr. Cermak's name is mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, as far as I recall, his name is not mentioned whatsoever. There is a mention of the -- of the garrisons in the Croatian Army, but I don't recall having come across Mr. Cermak's names -- name. Perhaps, yes, in the documents attached to The Blue Book, but in The Blue Book itself, I don't remember having seen Mr. Cermak's name. This was an analysis of Operation Storm. Did he not participate in Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to look at an extract of page 353 of the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could that be put on the ELMO so that everyone can see it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and that someone reads it aloud so that we have immediately already an impression of what The Blue Book, in this respect, says. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I haven't actually -- other than seeing a bound copy of The Blue Book, I haven't had a chance to really look at it, number one. Number two, the witness actually hasn't even, as far as I know, confirmed that that is what he was referring to, in terms of what was produced or anything. Just showing a page now, and Mr. Kay is identifying it without the witness identifying. I just raise the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just -- yes. Mr. Kay is in possession of what is called The Blue Book in, apparently, an electronic version, since yesterday. I take it that what Mr. Kay is putting on the ELMO is a passage of the document he received yesterday and which was presented to him as The Blue Book, and for the parties, for the next three months, to engage in battles about whether this is The Blue Book or not or whether it should be called The Red Book. But it's the complete Blue Book, etc. Mr. Feldi is now here; it's on the record, and let's be very practical. If there's any reason upon further studying the matter that this would not be part of The Blue Book, of course, that would be of influence to the evaluation of this evidence. It's clear what is now put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I apologise Mr. President. I think maybe I wasn't clear. The issue wasn't whether or not Mr. Kay has copied a page from what he is referring to as The Blue Book. My question was whether or not this witness is going to identify that from which it was copied as in fact that which he referred to during his testimony. That's the part I wasn't clear about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could ask him about that at a later stage. What would be appropriate to ask him at this moment is at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Always grateful to my learned friends behind me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I will get page 353 of The Blue Book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's now -- it appears in a format which might be recognised by the witness. Mr. Feldi, looking at what Mr. Kay has in his hands at this moment, would that look more or less what you know as being The Blue Book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already said that I'm not familiar with it, under the name of The Blue Book. But in any case, that's the material that I worked on. I don't know who named it The Blue Book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is this the analysis on Operation Oluja you referred to earlier? Work product --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's put that -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a copy like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's put this page on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. My team have kindly photocopied it for me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have now put -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... more complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Court establishes at this moment that it is not a single page which is put on the ELMO, but that it is a part of a voluminous book with a blue cover. And you said, Mr. Kay, it was page ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 353, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you look at page 353.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we can just move it up the screen, please, to there. No, not too high, please, to the part where it mentions -- there. Just stop. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Is there any portion that you would like to be read, then we will find a native B/C/S speaking person. Perhaps you could read it. And Mr. Kay will tell you where to start. And if you slowly read, we will understand what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you read the part that I marked on the photocopy, not wishing to mark the book. Please -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you read that out.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. "On the 5th of August, 1995, the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, by virtue of his decision referenced in footnote 572, appointed reserve Colonel General Ivan Cermak as commander of the Knin garrison. The former Knin garrison commander, Brigadier Marko Gojevic ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Major Marko Gojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... "is being appointed deputy garrison commander." This is the end of that part of the text, Your Honour. In the footnote we see that it refers to the decision of the president dated the 5th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is in evidence before this Court. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kay's question was whether I remember General Cermak being mentioned in the book. I cannot recall that, but having seen this, I can confirm that this is actually a part of the text that I had written in the book. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Kay, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are there any other references to General Cermak, so far as you know, in the book?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I do not recall that. I haven't seen the book for the past two or three years. Once I received a copy, I did go through it, but I put it aside afterwards. If there is any other reference, I cannot recall it. Perhaps you can jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I will save the Court time by not asking you to read it and confirm anything, and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But I have asked for a stipulation, Your Honour, on this matter that it was not forthcoming on the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The easiest way, Mr. Carrier, I think to see whether such stipulation could be engaged into would be electronic version of the advantage of being searchable. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: General -- no, General Cermak [sic], we're moving on from this. I want to ask you further questions on other matters, so put away the book please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps would it be good to have the hard copy to be given to the Prosecution so that they --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, it's the possession --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: yes, but therefore I'm inquiring whether it would be a good idea that since the book is now here. Mr. Mikulicic, any problem in giving it for a second in the hands of Mr. Carrier? He will certainly return it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No problem at all. But just to inform Your Honour, during the break, we produced and gave the book to Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But nevertheless, Mr. Carrier is also [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on. I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President, I understand that it was handed to Mr. Hedaraly and handed it back. Just -- we don't have a physical copy of the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If anyone wants to have the book in his hands, he is supposed to rise and then Madam Usher will assist us. Please proceed, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were asked various questions concerning the production of your report, one I want to ask you about. Were you ever instructed to write about Operation Oluja as part of your expert report for the Cermak Defence?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If any party had served a notice on you, requiring you to give evidence about Operation Oluja in these proceedings, would you have been pleased to do so?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I'm afraid that I didn't quite understand. In the event who exactly sought my statement? The gentleman present in the courtroom or in general terms? Because I was, in fact, called by the police in Zagreb to talk about the Operation Storm and also on the issue of artillery log-books; whereas, none of the parties to these proceedings ever got in touch with me or tried to make any sort of influence over me, in relation to Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to your expert report, were you given a page limitation by the Cermak Defence?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was one given as an approximation, but it was up to me to decide exactly how I was going formulate my views. And for that reason, in fact, the first version was a voluminous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were asked questions concerning General Lausic. Did you attend court to listen to his live evidence in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did you come to consider the testimony of General Lausic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I followed his testimony online on my computer at home. I made notes of his testimony, and I paid careful attention to his -- to it. General Lausic is an old friend of mine, comrade-in-arms. There were some parts of his testimony that came as a surprise to me, and for that reason, I made additional searches for certain documents to check whether what he was indeed saying was true. The documents proved him wrong, and that's why I used the documents to show how the system worked in practice. And that the HV commanders were not in command of MP units, save for those for which authorisation was given to an HV commander to have command over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is not for the first time that I hear this evidence. I think we've heard it already quite a number of times. Mr. Kay, you just asked how he was able to follow. It was apparently through the Internet. That's the answer to the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you consider the exhibits produced through General Lausic in relation to his evidence?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to the issue of de facto control or de jure control, do you appreciate the distinction?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I do understand. Regulations are one thing, and practice is quite another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to General Cermak, are you able to describe, in relation to his position, de facto and de jure, what his authority was?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- if you want to object to the question - is that what you intend to do? - then I would first like to hear the question in its entirety. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question as we may have lost of thread of it, General. In relation to General Cermak, are you able to give your opinion as to his de facto and de jure position as commander of the Knin garrison?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
