utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The objection is this is not proper re-examination. This is things that Mr. Feldi covered in his report. It was a question that was available to Mr. Kay during his in-chief. He submitted the report. It's not clear that this is an issue which is requiring re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- it's -- your objection is denied, Mr. Carrier. The witness may answer the question. Are you able to give your opinion as to the de facto and de jure position of Mr. Cermak as commander of the Knin garrison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can, and I will try to do it in as few words as possible. According to the regulations that were binding on the garrison commander, the organisational order of 1994 and the appended instructions, as well as the rules of service of the armed forces, a number of tasks were defined which the garrison commander was duty-bound to perform, from regulating matters through his instructions, supervision and coordination, and supervision of the tasks performed in -- within the garrison. These were the regulations. De facto, in practice, in the Knin garrison, out of all of tasks that were provided for a garrison commander, the garrison commander, Mr. Cermak, did not have as much as 20 per cent. There was no bathhouse, no river, seas or lakes. No public transportation, no sports terrains or storage facilities. All these issues that were mentioned in the instructions, he didn't know what the HV units were present in Knin because they changed constantly. He did not receive a single piece of information as to which of the HV units in the Knin garrison are available to provide officers and non-commissioned officers to organise duty service, to organise maintenance of order and discipline, or to provide security for certain facilities. All these matters were prescribed de jure as obligatory duties of the garrison commander. However, in practice in Knin at the time when General Cermak was there, all these and other conditions were not in place. He was in fact unable to implement the regulations, because he did not receive instructions, decisions or orders necessary to that effect. Let's me finish with one example. Not a single facilitate in the Knin garrison or in the town of Knin by virtue of the ministry's decision or the department for construction was given to be used by the Knin garrison as they wished which, under the rules, under the regulations they were duty-bound to do as was the case in other garrisons in Croatia, which had their storage facilities, barracks, re -- factories, kitchens, et cetera. What -- this is, in my view, the state of matters with regard do the de facto and de jure situation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, any further need to re-cross or to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, briefly, Mr. President. Further cross-examination by Mr. Misetic:

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Good morning again, General Feldi.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps before we start, there are one or two outstanding issues which perhaps we better deal with before we conclude the testimony. That is, first of all, the two documents, two documents for which Mr. Feldi would phone whatever authority - I'm saying it in this neutral way - I do understand that -- I was informed by the Registry that they expected to receive a copy of the two documents being faxed to The Hague, that the first attempt failed, that then there was more telephone conversation and that finally we would except now to have received a copy of these two documents. Mr. Registrar, could you inform us as to whether, now, at 11.45, copies were received by telefax.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, unfortunately, we haven't received them yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which comes a bit as a surprise, because in telephone conversation it was said that at the other end of the line that copies would be faxed. But, Mr. Feldi, any further information as to when we could expect these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I contacted the Ministry of Defence yesterday, as promised. They, in their turn, promised to send the telefax. I checked this morning and found that there was nothing coming. I phoned the ministry again and asked them to speed up the process and to make sure that the facsimile arrived before the end of my testimony. I was informed that the state secretary and his chief of the department -- of the department which holds the documentation were not there. The employees of the ministry told me that the documents could be found in the database of the ministry, and that they would do their best to send the documents to us as soon as possible. I don't know if complications can occur, since I did ask that the state secretary make sure that no such complications arise. You can have -- can you look at the document. You will see on the cover page the purpose for which the documentation was made and the list of all of us who produced the paper, and I apologise for the fact that the documents are still not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps yu should have phoned your wife, Mr. Feldi, and I don't know for sure whether that would have had a better result, but that is not for me to decide, although there was a strong suggestion in this direction yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so, Your Honour. My wife wouldn't know where to find my papers or where to begin to look for them. That's not her job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I leave it to the parties. At this moment the documents are not there. I can imagine that we can live without them and that most likely there would no objection to these documents being tendered from the bar table if they would show anything that the Chamber should be aware of. Mr. Carrier, is that approach a professional approach?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see no objections from the Defence side. Mr. Misetic, I wanted to have this clarified before we continued. Please now continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: General Feldi, I just wanted to go back to some questioning that concluded with the Presiding Judge putting the matter to you, and this is at page 28, beginning at line 16, going on to page 29, through line 4. And you'll recall that earlier this morning there was a discussion about Article 9 and whether the absence of further regulations could be interpreted either to mean that Article 9 was self-executing as evidenced by the absence of further regulations, or whether, as you say, the absence of further regulations meant that Article 9 was not self-executing? And my question to you, on the basis of your report, goes to this issue. The Chamber has received in evidence many orders from General Lausic from beginning of 1995 through the end of 1995, and one such example is Exhibit D267, from the 2nd of August, 1995, where General Lausic, in his order, will put that, for example, The military police for daily operational tasks is subordinated to the commanders of... and then amongst other things it says, Military Districts. Now, my question to you, General Feldi, is: If, in fact, Article 9 was in effect and was self-executing, would there have been any purpose to General Lausic then having to issue further orders talking about or ordering subordination to HV commanders, if, in fact, Article 9 on its face was applicable and self-executing?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the 2nd of August document is where the matters that you referred to were regulated. On the very following day another task is issued within the area of responsibility of Major Juric who is given all the powers to have authority over the military police. So basically there is the order which is implemented, and on the 5th, Juric is sending a report whereby the system is working and he is in commands of all -- of all the military police units, including the MP company, stationed in Knin. We need go no further than the documents themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activate]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I appreciate your answer, General Feldi, and I didn't mean to go into the specifics surrounding the 2nd of August order, I was using that as one example. But there are other examples. Let's take it out of the context of Operation Storm, General Feldi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, sorry to interrupt you. Could you -- the 2nd of August document is six pages. Could you refer to a specific paragraph so that we can focus on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's page 4 of 6 in the English in e-court, paragraph 12, first bullet point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: General Feldi, my question was would you agree with me that if Article 9 was in effect and was self-executing from February 1994, there would have been no need for General Lausic to issue his own orders throughout 1994 and 1995 concerning, for example, daily -- or daily operational chain of command in subordinating them, because it would have already been regulated by Article 9 of the rules? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Misetic, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Misetic. Mr. Carrier, any furthers questions for Mr. Feldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do have one given my ten minutes with The Blue Book which I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, well, at least I'm glad that my suggestion leads to something. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: We'll see how it goes but ... My question is, and I haven't had a full opportunity to look into it, so I'm not sure -- sorry. If I could just have one moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Perhaps I could just ask a clarifying question. Further cross-examination by Mr. Carrier:

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, if you turn to page -- or I will give you the section number. It's 1.3.7.3. And in your original version of your report, it is labeled as organigram number 12, Command in the Croatian Army, 4 August 1995. Now I just want to clarify a few things. I believe today when you looked at the bound copy of The Blue Book, which you can see is this book here. I think you said you hadn't seen it in two or three years, and you can correct me if I'm wrong, but my understanding from your evidence yesterday is that you didn't -- as far as you know, you didn't rely or use anything from that Blue Book when you produced your report for General Cermak. Is that a fair interpretation of your position on that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could ask that something be placed on sanction. I don't speak Croatian, but I do have -- I made a slight interpretation of this organigram -- or on ELMO, sorry. It is something from The Blue Book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the assistance of Madam Usher, it can be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And while that's being put on, Mr. Registrar, if could you bring up the Croatian version of Mr. Feldi's report and if could you find the organigram, which is the top right-hand side corner, pages are numbered, it's 2618, I could be wrong. And I'm not sure -- in English, at least, it's -- at the top of the version I have it's 2618. And the organigram is entitled: System of command in the Croatian Army, Operation Storm, 4 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And if the -- if Madam Usher could adjust it slightly so that we could also see the Croatian version of Mr. Feldi's report, and I don't know if it's possible to put the ELMO image up on the screen at the same time. Sorry, just to be clear, just the Croatian version of the organigram in the report. I apologise to you, Mr. Registrar. I know he is trying to find it. And I'll see if I can find it quickly. I believe it is on page -- the bottom of page 14 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it -- it takes quite a while. Mr. Carrier, may I take it that you would like to ask the witness to compare what we find in his report to what we find The Blue Book.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's your suggestion that it's the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's ... Could you have a look at what we find in The Blue Book and what we find in your report, could you compare and see whether it's the same or approximately the same? Mr. Feldi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's roughly the same. It's my diagram. It dates back from the time when I worked on the analysis of Operation Storm. It's one of the diagrams or organigrams. There are several of them, and some of them ended up in this book. I used it deliberately because this system of command was in place in the Croatian Army at the time when General Cermak arrived in the Knin garrison. In order to demonstrate that in this -- under this system of command, there are no garrisons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, I don't think that Mr. Carrier is interested at this moment in whether there were garrisons or not. But what he apparently wanted to know is whether you relied on The Blue Book in preparing the report, in contradiction to your earlier testimony. Mr. Carrier, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I took it from your answer that The Blue Book relied on your diagrams rather than that you relied on the diagrams that were published in The Blue Book. Did you keep electronic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you keep electronic copies of the diagrams you produced before The Blue Book was published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't do it in the electronic form. I did them by hand, for the most part. And I have many diagrams in my notebooks and various drafts. I did not produce it electronically because there are people who have the -- the necessary expertise. I drew them by hand and then others processed them. The difference between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you a follow-up question here. You produced them by land, although I read in your CV that you followed a course in computer science, but here you relied on others to produce what apparently is an electronically produced diagram. Would you agree with that? When did you give -- I saw you nodding yes. When did you give your handwritten diagram to those who then turned it into in an electronic version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when we were working on this material, I gave them my working organigram. It was slightly changed, as you can see, in the book. There is a significant difference between the one used in my text and the one in the book. And by your leave, I can point out two elements that are different. We find them in the organigram in the book and they are missing in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning the book organigram, there is a separate piece of text that you can see, stating that full command authority over the units of the military police was in the hands of the MP administration of MOD, whilst commanders of the Military Districts had the authority of operational command and control over those military police units of that were assigned to them. This piece of text is missing in my report. Further down it says, Operational teams of the Main Staff of the armed forces had the task to convey orders issued by the Chief of Staff, monitor the situation, receive reports, carry out assessments, draft new orders and pass them down to the subordinates. This sentence is also not in my expert report. To continue, if I may, in this text, it says, For the needs of operational oversight a separate command post was established in Ogulin. In my organigram, that was my draft, and I -- I used it during the operation. I didn't make up a single thing. This is just slightly changed to have a clear layout, and I have told you what the reason was for the differences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could I try to establish what exactly happened with you had a handwritten diagram drafted? When did you give it to those who produced this electronic version? The electronic version as we find it in The Blue Book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in 2006, I believe, while we were working on the book, because I worked with the team for at least half of 2007 as well, and this is when we were agreeing upon the structure, et cetera. One of the things we discussed was, among other things, this organigram that concerns itself with the command structure of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, how did you obtain for yourself an electronic version, if you ever obtained such an electronic version, of what you gave to them in a handwritten form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received a copy, Your Honour. It was printed out for me so that I could use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When did you receive that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was when we discussed the material prepared for the book, before its final form took shape. I provided my organigram to those who were supposed to make the layout and then they gave me a hard copy so that I could take it back home to review it and use it during the meetings in the Central Archives. After that, this organigram was handed over together with the rest of the material, and it was put in the book. What I have is the copy I have been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever receive an electronic copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did you get -- in the original report, how did you work in this diagram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mm-hm. Your Honour, while working on the expert report, I contacted those in the Main Staff who had first put it in electronic form. I asked for it, and they gave me the version I had before. I never received it in electronic form but on -- in hard copy, as a schematic. I scanned it afterwards and put it in an electronic form. That's the version I have. I have no other. I don't have the organigram from the book in electronic form separately. It is only a part of the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we finds in the original - that is, the Croatian version of your report, and I think it is on page 14 - is that a scanned image of a diagram you received from, as you said - let me just check --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The people who put it in electronic form?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you received a hard copy from them. And then you scanned it, isn't it? Let me just check your last answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And included it in my report. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you never received it in an electronic form, but this is in this report as it is sent to us. This is a scanned image of a hard copy you received from the people in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know who I received it from, Your Honour. Those were people who used all of our hand-made schematics to put them into the computer. They had it stored as a working version, and as such was given to me. Later on it was amended and changed by suggestions of other team members, and they added the text I mentioned as well as a number of boxes whenever they found my schematic lacking. Such as an amended version as you can find it in The Blue Book is not something I used in my expert report. You can see that for yourselves because of the differences I pointed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see your point that there are differences. Perhaps I would like -- what I would like to know specifically is whether the diagram which we find in the original of your report is the product of scanning and putting that image into this section of the report. When thinking about the answer, perhaps I ask you: Did you scan it at home? Did you -- where did you scan it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where did you scan it then, if not at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the office, where I worked with the rest of the team on the preparation of the report. Not only this particular organigram, but all others as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said in the office where you worked preparing the report. Which report are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My expert report. My expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which office was that where you worked with the rest of the team to prepare this report? Which office was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Zagreb. In the premises where the team was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber received the hard copy of the report. Is there an electronic version? I -- it may be that we have received it also on a CD. Is that ... Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's filed electronically and created electronically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Filed electronically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If Your Honour is doing the questioning, perhaps invite you to ask which team is he referring to so that there is no ambiguity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, I was still in the middle of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So there's no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for the suggestion, Mr. Kay. What team were you talking about, Mr. Feldi, when you scanned it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I was a bit unclear. As of last year, I was made a team member for Defence of General Cermak. I was asked to join and assist with that part that I'm familiar with. I was in Knin, and I could be of assistance to Mr. Kay, to get acquainted with the situation as quickly as possible. I joined the, what was called, Croatian part of the team that was in Zagreb. Together with the Knin part of the team, we worked on the analysis of the documentation that may be of assistance to General Cermak's Defence. And I was supposed to acquaint Mr. Kay and the rest of his Hague team. This is where I also worked on the expert report, relying on the technical services and support that I needed to produce that report. I used the database that the team had, containing the documents that I used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, I intervened at a moment where you started some questions. I very much focussed on the genesis of how these diagrams were produced, et cetera. I'm aware that I interrupted you. I'm not saying that I would have no further questions, but I would rather first allow to further develop the questions you would like to put to Mr. Feldi, and meanwhile we'll give it some thought on whether we have further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I guess sometimes a picture is worth a thousand words. I don't really want to ask any questions about this. I think it's clear on the face of the document. The one issue, perhaps, that might clarify things is at the Prosecution's request Mr. Kay had sent colour versions of the organigrams used in Mr. Feldi's report. I have a copy of this specific one, which I'm happy to supply in terms of just to reference it. The other thing is since we have a hard copy of a signed original Blue Book here at the moment, and I understand that we have been given a CD of that book, the Prosecution clearly hasn't had a chance to compare the two and make sure everything is there in the same way. I think out of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are differences as the witness told us and as the witness showed us, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: That's -- obviously, alarm bells are ringing. And so we're asking that The Blue Book be admitted into hard copy, The Blue Book also be admitted as an exhibit so that we have a version of now preserved while it has been referred to in Court by this witness, et cetera. It just makes more sense in Prosecution's submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just the hard copy or the electronic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: At least now, definitely the hard copy. And what the Prosecution is submitting for Your Honours' consideration is that we would scan the individual pages of the hard copy book if Mr. Kay would like it back, and, at the same time, perhaps also file or file the electronic version as well, just so that we have a complete record of what this document is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's not my copy of the book, actually, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour. I thought that was perfectly clear that this is my copy of The Blue Book, not Mr. Kay's. So I'm not willing to The Blue Book into the evidence. If my learned colleague from the Prosecution side wants to enter this into evidence, let him copy the book and let do with the copies whatever they want. But the original book that I was giving to them, it's not the one that I want to produce it into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, once an exhibit is admitted into evidence, it will be for the future in the custody of the Tribunal and not available to the owner anymore. The suggestion by Mr. Mikulicic that you would prepare copies of it and then everyone now, apart from the Chamber, has seen from nearby The Blue Book and then to tender the copies into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps that's the best solution. If we could scan it first and then look at it, and then determine the best way of dealing with it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, scanning is another word for copying, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, do you remember -- do you remember the discussions where your original diagram was completed or changed into the version we now find on the -- in The Blue Book?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall when, Your Honour. There were many diagrams and many things discussed. The final version that can you find in The Blue Book, as I have said already, was worked on by all of us together, and I don't remember when we produced the final version of it, as can you find it in The Blue Book. If I may, I did not enter those subsequent changes into my copy in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I come back to my earlier question, whether, as you said, the hard copy you received from the -- from the team preparing the Oluja analysis, whether you scanned that, whether you are sure about that. You told us already where it was scanned. Are you sure that it was scanned and then put into your report?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try to be more precise. The diagram was originally done by hand. When we were discussing the book with the team at the Main Staff or in the archives, I handed over that diagram, and then it was used by our IT support to put it in electronic form, in that type of layout. After that, the diagram they put in the electronic form was discussed. That copy of the diagram, based on my handwritten one, is the one that I have in the book. When the final version was being discussed, in terms of what should be added or taken away from the diagram, because if you look at some other diagrams, can you see that they have some elements or missing some other elements that the others don't have. This diagram is something that I used to try to prove that this was indeed the system of command. The copy that I received in printed form from the Main Staff is what I asked to have so that I could attach it, and so I did. It not actual -- an actual scan of my handwritten diagram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did understand your testimony to be that you received a printed out version of an electronically produced copy of your original handwritten diagram and that you then scanned that printout, or hard copy, and then that the result of this scan was introduced in your report. Could I ask you, did you -- the report, was that type written by yourself or by anyone else?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was typing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you were the one who introduced the scanned diagrams into this text.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would did then that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the diagram I received from the Main Staff, I worked on some other diagrams as well, and it was put in electronic form by the personnel of the office for General Cermak's Defence, the team members. My IT background is lacking. It is not sufficient for me to produce such complicated diagrams in electronic form. Usually I would make them in handwriting and then would hand them over, so that they would do the graphic design. The same thing happened with the Main Staff. I asked -- I brought in my copy, and it was scanned in the office. Later on, I was able to use that diagram in my part of the text, much as many other diagrams that I used in working version. Some of them are contained in the report as well. That was the procedure that I employed when working on this expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me now try to understand. You received from the Main Staff a printout, a printout, which, you said, was then scanned. At the same time, you tell us that you gave your copy - whether that was the printout or the already-scanned copy - to the team members of the Cermak Defence team in order to produce them in an electronic format. That's at least how I understood your last -- because you said it was not the scanned version that was put into your report, but it was an electronic version produced by the Cermak Defence team on the basis of the hard copies you had available, and that, due to your lack of IT experience, they put that in the text you had type-written. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there seems to be a misunderstanding. I will try to make it simple. On my request, the Main Staff gave me a copy of the diagram I had produced when producing the document ation. They had that diagram in the computer. They printed it out. I received a paper, a piece of paper. That printed text is what I handed over in the office to the team I worked with. They scanned it and entered it into their database. When I was working on my expert report, I used the database diagram and put it in the text, and you see the result before you. I only assisted them when they were working on it to have it in the layout as envisaged originally. I don't have it in electronic form. I can only access it from the database.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, your answers create some confusion with me. You said "they scanned it," the document, "and they put it in the database." And then you said, I used the database diagram and put it in the text. So you used, from what I understand, the diagram as it was stored in the database; and you put it in your text. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, therefore, it was still a scanned copy, and it was not a diagram which was recreated electronically?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you're talking about working with the team members and being assisted by the team. And you said something about -- let me just check carefully what you said. Let me just see ... One second, please. You said you were made a team member for the Defence. Did you perform any other duties than to produce this expert report?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was one of the advisors on the team, based on my experience and work in the Croatian Army and knowledge of these events. They believed that I could provide useful advice and suggestions, as well as make sure that Mr. Kay and his team get apprised of all the matters as soon as possible. That was the reason why I was included in the team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your duties went beyond producing an expert report.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, these duties preceded my work on this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The instruction to produce an expert report, or the request to produce an expert report was given to you after you had already been advising the team. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you work on the report on the premises where the team was working at that moment?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I partly worked at home and partly on the premises where the team worked. The team did not work round the clock, 24 hours, and I would therefore spend the evenings working at home, and I would roughly spend between three to four hours on the premises of the team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, your diagrams are not exactly the same as the ones which we find in The Blue Book. You've told us that the final analysis was approved by the Main Staff, the analysis that appears in The Blue Book. Did you, in your report, anywhere explain why your diagrams and the content of it deviate from the version that was prepared for the Ministry of Defence, approved by the Main Staff, and, finally, published in The Blue Book?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, nowhere in my report did I comment on this particular diagram and on the diagrams I used in general. The diagrams included in the report were not published in The Blue Book, as they stand now, and I didn't feel the need to account for any difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What's your assessment of the importance of the difference in the diagram we just looked at in your report and the one which was public -- was published The Blue Book? Would you consider this a minor difference; or would it be relevant to one of the issues that was subject to your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can confirm that this is the diagram that I produced with minor differences that I referred to. If you will allow me, the purpose of the diagram is to show the system of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi, I'm asking you specifically whether you considered the difference between the diagram, as published in The Blue Book, and the diagram, as produced in your report, is of minor importance or touches upon matters that seemed to be of relevance during your examination in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the diagram published in The Blue Book would have been more appropriately used, had it been put in my report, or, rather it would have been a more appropriate choice, because it is a more complete form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although that is not an answer to my question, I leave it to that. Mr. Feldi, your role as an advisor in the Cermak Defence team, is this to be found in your CV; and, if so, please assist me in finding it.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, I didn't include it my resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Don't you think that it could have been of relevance to know whether you were engaged in other activities of the Defence team? Just as we know, for example, from Prosecutor experts, whether they are employed by the Prosecution or engaged in their activities. Did you consider this irrelevant, or was there any other reason why you didn't mention it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO FELDI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you will allow me to say this, I didn't mention that I was on the team for the book intended for General Markac, and equally so, I didn't mention my participation in the team for General Cermak. There was no particular reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Have the questions by the Bench triggered any need to further examine the witness? That should be after a break, but if not, then we could conclude before the break. If there are any further questions, then they should be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have nothing for my part. Nothing arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I see that that's true for all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to receive in evidence the electronic copy of The Blue Book, and I think the electronic copy of the expert report was provided to the Chamber but is not specifically admitted into evidence in that format. Is that correct, Mr. Kay? We have received the hard copy as ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it is filed electronically and that's the version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the version --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, we all have the same version. Your Honour has not got any different version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not saying that we -- I'm just for purposes of at least having an opportunity to compare The Blue Book, electronic version, with the electronic version of the expert report, I just wanted to be sure that the electronic version is, as such, available. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As I said before, perhaps additional information that would assist is that Mr. Kay provided the Prosecution at our request colour versions of the organigrams themselves, which I think would be better given that they're -- The Blue Book has colour diagrams, and these are the colour diagrams provided that were referenced in the report, so I could give those over if there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if they are part of what has been filed, and I do understand that the electronic version including the colours, has been filed, then there is no need to -- then it is only the electronic version of The Blue Book that we would like to have in evidence. And we leave it to you, Mr. Carrier, whether you want to have a photocopied version of The Blue Book in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I think, sorry, the issue is that the electronic version that was filed as his report is a scanned version which doesn't reproduce the colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it a scanned version that is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As to that, I'm unsure. But we will serve another electronic version -- on the Court. But ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we would like to have -- apparently, this report has been produced under some kind of Word programme or whatever it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you can make it an image by scanning it. And then of course we also have an electronic version but of a different kind compared to the original version which is the version in which you can change letters, if you want to, I'm not suggesting that even, but that's a version in which you can work. Whereas, a scanned version is just a series of, I would say, photographs, of pages, which cannot be worked on anymore, unless you apply OCR, which is optical character recognition and then get it back from a picture, from an image, to a text or a file which contains text, and, for example portions of databases or whatever. And what the Chamber would like to have is a version of the report not as an image but as it was produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, yes, we can go to the database and get you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I have to apologise for taking far too much time and also not considering that we needed a break. Mr. Feldi, there are no further questions for you. I would like to thank you for coming to The Hague and for answering all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe journey home again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for hearing me out, and I wish you success in your future work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Feldi. Madam Usher, could you escort Mr. Feldi out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are a few procedural matters which we cannot deal with now which would take me approximately five to -- well, I would say ten minutes to deal with. That means that the time remaining would be 25 minutes. Mr. Kay, in view of the testimony of Mr. Feldi, which was introduced, his expert report was introduced in a very quick way, I take it that it would make sense to have the next witness to appear, even if is only for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We will have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly apparently left. We are still waiting to hear --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption, Your Honour, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sorry for being too impatient, Mr. Registrar. We are -- no. Mr. Hedaraly tendered 65 ter 7395. And Mr. Kehoe, although the -- said, as it reads on the transcript that, If he could just have a diplomat, I took it to be a minute, but we are still waiting for your response to the tendering of 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My objection to that document - I'd looked back - was based on my objection to some other documents which came into evidence, so we withdraw our objection concerning that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Registrar, could a number be assigned to 65 ter 7395, tendered by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2634.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Then, finally, as the parties may remember, I stopped halfway in a decision on the admission of 11 witness statements, pursuant to Rule 92 bis because it seems that there was a confusing text for me at that time. I now return, then, to the Chamber's decision on part of the Gotovina Defence's motion for admission of 11 witness statements, pursuant to Rule 92 bis. When reading out its decision, the Chamber indicated that it would come back to discuss the dates on which the exhibit numbers were assigned to the witness statements. This discussion can be found on transcript pages 21.783 through 21.786, and the Chamber would now like to clarify the dates on which the statements and corresponding exhibit numbers were given. The Registrar has informally told the Chamber that the attestations for each of the seven 92 bis statements will be added to the exhibit numbers previously assigned to each of these statements. And the following statements were assigned exhibit numbers in court, on the 16th of May, 2009; the statement of Davor Perisa given on the 9th May 2008 was assigned exhibit number D195; the statement of Boris Filipovic given on the 9th May 2008 was assigned the exhibit number D196; the statement Srecko Grubisic given on the 8th of May 2008 was assigned exhibit number D198; the statement of Jordan Tudic given on the 8th of May 2008, was assigned exhibit number D199; and the statement of Josip Elez given on the 8th of May 2008, was assigned exhibit number D202. The following statements were assigned exhibit numbers in court on 19th May, 2009. The statement of Ratko Despot, given on the 18th of May 2008, was assigned exhibit number D206; the statement of Tihomir Mis given on the 18th of May 2008, was assigned exhibit number D207; and accordingly, as already stated on the record, D195, D196, D198, D199, D202, D206, and D207 were admitted into evidence. And this concludes the Chamber's clarification on this matter. Mr. Kay, are you ready to call your next witness, which I understand will be Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. There is just one matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The matters Your Honour raised just before the short adjournment. You have been given this in an OCR'd format, which is searchable. That is how the Cermak Defence supplied the English version of this document to the Trial Chamber. So you have a searchable document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is not only my concern about whether it would be searchable or not; it was just an explanation. What the Chamber sought was to receive the document as it was produced. Now, if you produce a document, you then scan it. With OCR you can make it a searchable document again. Even some of the scanned documents are searchable. It is not whether it is searchable or not but is about how it was produced, which interested the Chamber most. If you please consider that within your team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour understands that it's a Croatian language document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Fine. That was my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was concerned with other matters whether -- and I knew I had given instructions that these reports could be searchable to assist everybody, and that was that. But the document produced by General Feldi is in the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we understood that he had type-written himself, I take it, through a word processor, the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And as he told us he included or inserted in his text the copy of the diagrams he had given in hard copy, which were then stored in an electronic database and of which he had never received an electronic copy of the Main Staff and which was then inserted in his text. That is what, in brief, the matter which the Chamber is interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will endeavour to produce that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Madam Usher, could you escort the next witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kovacevic. Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration, that you speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Kovacevic, the text will now be handed out to you. Could I invite to you make at that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Mr. Kovacevic. I noticed that you have brought a large bag with -- I take it, is full of documents. If you would want to consult them, would you please address the Court so that we are aware that are you consulting any of these documents and whether, looking at the bag, this goes to weight or to admissibility, is, looking at the bag, weight certainly will be important. You will first be examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is your name Pero Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Pero Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And were you instructed to me to produce an expert witness report in this case?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You instructed me to put together an expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May the Court produce 65 ter 2D00-734 for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, on the screen in front of you, you will see in your own language, as well as the English language, the front page of an expert report by you. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And can you confirm that you handed that report over to me for filing in this case as an expert witness report?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the expert witness report of Mr. Kovacevic be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask for permission to reserve our position until after the Prosecution has an opportunity to cross on transparency and methodology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, could you please assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become exhibit number D1676, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do the other Defence teams already want to express their position in relation to this report? Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have no remarks on that report, so -- as it concerns to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So admission is not a problem for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We have no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's on the record. The Chamber will decide at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is also a corrigendum to the document with five corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could 65 ter 2D00-745 be put onto the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document in the English language. Mr. Kovacevic, do you speak English and read English?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Not to the extent which would enable me to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll notice a number of details on this piece of paper, and they concern corrections to your report. Do you confirm that you submitted to us a series of corrections of a minor nature to your report to enable it to be more accurate?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that. More or less, these were just typographical errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, might this be marked for identification following the previous submission for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and its fate depends on the previous -- on the expert report itself. Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become exhibit number D1677, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am informed, just for references which I should point out now, that in the English language version there has been a typographical error. At page 43, 3.2.97, and missing is the two words "active duty," where there is the typescript of military person. The Croatian has the original Croatian language of Mr. Kovacevic, with the phrase for "active duty." It's been missed off on the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I hope that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, do you confirm the contents of your expert opinion report as submitted to this Court?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do confirm the contents of my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In those circumstances, Your Honour, I have no further questions to ask of ask. Mr. Kovacevic is available for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have a few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A few questions. We have seven minutes left. Do you think we could deal with them or?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's give it a try. Mr. Kovacevic you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention to paragraph 3.2.8 of your report. In that section you stated that: "Military persons shall continue to be responsible for disciplinary violations committed during their service in the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, even after termination of service." In your opinion, does that provision also apply to persons who had been mobilized into the HV and then had been demobilized?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: This provision could also be applied in the cases of all those COs and NCOs who had been mobilized into the armed forces and committed disciplinary violations. After having been demobilized, they could be subjected to disciplinary proceedings with different results, such as staggered promotion, and other consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What about mobilized persons who were not mobilized COs and NCOs?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Our situation was rather peculiar, because we had a reserve force which had been mobilized, and was in active duty. They were a constituent part of the armed forces. There was the obligatory military term of those conscripts who had to serve that term, and they were mobilized during the period of an immediate threat to the stability and unity of the state. It was necessary to increase the discipline and reputation of the armed forces. But first and foremost, we were trying to focus on the active duty personnel. If the active duty personnel is well disciplined, that is a guarantee that the reserve force during their service with the armed forces would be respected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I got the impression from Mr. Misetic's question that he would like to know what would happen if a -- not a commissioned -- or a non-commissioned officer but another serviceman would be demobilized and whether this provision would still apply, rather than to know the background and ... Could you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could be used only seldom in that case. Because these were reserve soldiers against which one cannot initiate a disciplinary procedure when they have committed an offence, only disciplinary procedure in cases of breaches or violations of discipline could be instituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That leads me to my next question, Mr. Kovacevic. With respect to a member of the HV who was mobilized into the HV, under your understanding of the rules, could a mobilized member of the HV be brought before the military disciplinary court due to a major disciplinary violation?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: He could in cases of COs and NCOs, but that had to be established through a separate procedure. I don't know whether you need me to explain what the procedure was, once it was learned that a disciplinary violation was committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Time is sort, so let me see if I can finish today.

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My question specifically -- let's exclude COs -- commissioned officers and non-commissioned officers in mobilized units. In terms of an ordinary mobilized soldier, if he commits a major disciplinary violation, would he be brought before the military disciplinary court?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. According to the code of discipline, a mobilized soldier could not. He could only be held responsible for his disciplinary violations, which are minor breaches of discipline, not in cases of offences or major violations, as you termed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What happens to a mobilized soldier who committed what would amount to a major disciplinary breach? Was there a practice of what would happen to them?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: If we are talking about a soldier and there was a serious violation, and pronouncing a disciplinary measure, be it detention or other measure, detention being the most serious disciplinary measure, it -- if that is impossible, in such cases that person would be demobilized. If, other hand, that soldier was on active duty, then he would be suspended, provided that proceedings were instituted against him in case he had committed an offence, a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just to be clear, when you say that person was active duty, do you mean a professional soldier?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We have the active or professional side of the armed forces and the reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I have one final question, Mr. President. If we could go to section 5.1.7 of your report. You talk about the military police. And by way of background, you indicate that the 1994 rules removed from subordination to the Main Staff, Military District commands and units of the Croatian Army, the military police. In other words, if I can restate that, the 1994 rules removed the military police from the commands of the Main Staff, Military Districts, and units of the Croatian Army. Can you briefly tell us why that decision was taken, to remove military police units from the command of the army?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about amendments to the defence law from 1993. The military police was taken from the commands of the armed forces, and the military police was placed under the Ministry of Defence, and I can tell you later on how this was done. There were several reasons for the decision. The first reason was to increase military discipline and protect reputation, and we wanted to have an independent opinion of the military police that would not be part of the military forces, part of the units, but an outsider. That's how we wanted to prevent breaches of discipline. We followed a German model. The military police was part of the Ministry of Defence, and in Article 151 or 152 of the defence law, which was amended, provides for its specific role with regard to the military forces. The law, as I said, was amended in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. I may have one or more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then you have an opportunity. But I'm at risk to be disciplined if I stay any longer in this court, Mr. Misetic. Mr. Kovacevic, it was only very brief today. That will be different tomorrow. We'd like to see you back at 9.00 tomorrow morning in the same courtroom. And I want to instruct you that you should not speak about the testimony whether the small portion of evidence given today or what will follow in the days to come. So, therefore, would you please keep that in your mind. We adjourn, and we will resume tomorrow, Friday, the 25th of September, 9.00, Courtroom III.
